description: Since 1951, a rule has protected persecuted people around the world. But she did not foresee today's migration crises.

hero.hook: Since 1951, a rule has protected the persecuted throughout the world. But she didn't predict the climate.

blocks.text: All over the world, people are fleeing their countries because their lives or freedom are threatened. For centuries, an unwritten rule has been that we open a door for them: it is the **right of asylum**. Framed by specific laws since the 20th century, this gate is today increasingly contested.

The modern legal framework for asylum is based on the  of 1951, written after World War II, when millions of people were still wandering Europe. Originally limited to Europe, it became universal in 1967, thanks to an additional protocol. **[[Geneva Convention]]**

The Convention gives a precise definition of the word **refugee**: a person outside his country who cannot return there for fear of being persecuted for his race, his religion, his nationality, his membership in a social group, or his political opinions. This definition, disturbingly, excludes victims of natural disasters or famine.

The heart of this protection is called the principle of : it prohibits sending a person to a place where they would risk torture or death. The United Nations relies on the , an agency specializing in the protection of uprooted people, to ensure its application. **[[The principle of non-refoulement]]** **[[UNHCR]]**
We often imagine welcoming refugees as a burden for rich countries. Yet around 75% of the world's refugees are hosted by low- and middle-income countries located near conflict zones.

In public debates, the words migrant and refugee are often confused, but they designate different legal situations. A **asylum seeker** has submitted an application for protection and is waiting for an authority to examine it. If he gets a positive response, he officially becomes a **refugee**, with the right to stay permanently and work.

Conversely, a **economic migrant** leaves his country voluntarily to seek a better life, and the Geneva Convention does not apply to him. This distinction is a source of political tension, because the actual paths are often mixed, and the examination of an application can take several years, during which applicants often do not have the right to work.

sections.title: Refugee, asylum seeker, migrant: different words

blocks.text: The year **2015** marked a turning point for Europe: more than a million people crossed the Mediterranean Sea, mainly fleeing the civil war in Syria. This influx revealed the flaws of , which requires the first country of arrival to process each request, overburdening Greece and Italy. **[[Dublin Regulation]]**

blocks.caption: In 2015, more than a million people crossed the Mediterranean to reach Europe.

blocks.text: Faced with this crisis, Europe reacted in a dispersed manner. In 2016, an agreement between the EU and Turkey proposed a compromise: in exchange for financial aid, Turkey agreed to block departures to Europe, a strategy criticized for its possible disregard for non-refoulement. In 2024, the EU adopts a new pact on migration, seeking a balance between solidarity and border surveillance.

One of the most famous refugees in history is Albert Einstein. In 1933, threatened by the Nazis because of his Jewish origins, he renounced his German nationality and obtained asylum in the United States.

sections.title: 2015: the shock of the European migration crisis

blocks.text: The future of the right to asylum faces a reality that the drafters of 1951 had not foreseen: the climate crisis. By 2050, hundreds of millions of people could be displaced by rising seas or desertification, but climate refugee status still does not exist because these people cannot prove “persecution” under the Convention.

At the same time, asylum is becoming an increasingly politicized subject in Western democracies: procedures are becoming tougher, and the idea of ​​only temporary protection is gaining ground compared to that of lasting integration.

The 1951 Geneva Convention protects people persecuted for political, religious or social reasons, thanks to the principle of non-refoulement. But it remains unsuitable in the face of new flows of climate refugees and today's mixed migratory crises.

sections.title: The new challenge: climate and politicization
